name: Classic Motorcycle Mecca
description:
More than 300 classic and vintage motorcycles, the oldest from 1902, fill two restored heritage buildings on Tay Street in the city centre. The collection runs from Indian and Harley-Davidson bikes to British classics, Brough Superiors, motocross and speedway machines, with tributes to Burt Munro and Ivan Mauger and the George Begg Bunker, which honours the Southland engineer who built racing cars.

The bikes are displayed without glass cases, so you can get up close to the details, and there's an art gallery and the Kickstart Café on site. It's open daily from 10am to 5pm, and a Turbo Pass combines entry with Bill Richardson Transport World for a discount.
Local tip: Allow at least two hours if you like old bikes, since the collection takes longer to get through than it looks.
hoursNote: Daily 10am to 5pm; last entry 4pm; closed 25 and 26 December; paid entry

name: Stirling Point and Foveaux Walkway, Bluff
description:
The end of State Highway 1 at Bluff, 25km south of Invercargill, marked by the yellow signpost showing distances to the Equator, the South Pole and cities around the world. It's also where Te Araroa, the trail that runs the length of the country, finishes, and there are views over Foveaux Strait to Stewart Island, plus parking and public toilets.

The Foveaux Walkway runs along the coast from the signpost through low bush to Lookout Point, about 2 hours return, with panels on the history and wildlife of the strait. Fur seals haul out near the track in winter, and southern right whales are sometimes seen further out. You can return the same way or loop back through the bush on the Glory Track, past the historic gun pits. Parking by the sign is limited, and it's usually windy.
Local tip: If you're short on time, walk just the first 10 or 15 minutes of the walkway for the views, and look for the kelp beds swaying in the water below.
hoursNote: Open any time; limited parking at the signpost; exposed and windy

name: Bluff Hill Lookout (Motupōhue)
description:
The lookout on top of Bluff Hill, or Motupōhue, reached by a steep drive up Lee Street and Flagstaff Road from Stirling Point. A path leads up from the car park to the summit, where there's a 360 degree view over Foveaux Strait, Stewart Island, the port and the Southland plains.

Panels along the path cover the hill's natural history, its significance to Māori and its uses since European settlement. Walking tracks lead down the hill, including the Tōpuni Track to Stirling Point past WWII gun emplacements.
Local tip: Bring takeaways up for sunset on a clear evening, and check the weather first, since on a cloudy day you'll see very little.
hoursNote: Open any time; sealed road to the car park; very exposed in wind

name: Oreti Beach
description:
A very long, flat, open beach about 15 minutes west of Invercargill, where you can drive on the hard sand. Burt Munro practised his speed runs here, and the Burt Munro Challenge still holds beach races on the sand each February.

It's wild and uncrowded, and good for a walk and sunsets. Toheroa, a rare native shellfish, live near the high tide mark and are protected. The sea is cold and the surf can be rough.
Local tip: If you drive onto the beach, stick to the firm sand below the high tide mark, keep to the 30km/h speed limit, stay off the dunes, and watch for walkers, children and horses.
hoursNote: Open any time; vehicles allowed on the beach; check tides before driving on the sand

name: Old Hokonui Moonshine Museum
description:
A small museum in Gore's heritage precinct, about an hour northeast of Invercargill, telling the story of the illegal whisky that settlers made in the Hokonui Hills from the late 1800s, and of the prohibition and temperance years that followed. Displays, audio and artefacts show how the moonshiners kept ahead of the police.

Adults are $10, which includes a taste of moonshine distilled on site, and under 18s get in free, though under 12s need an adult with them. Guided tours are $20 and must be booked. The entrance is on Norfolk Street, and you pay at the Gore Visitor Centre at the front.
Local tip: It's closed on Sundays and public holidays and shuts at 2pm on Saturdays, so plan around that, then walk a few steps to the free Eastern Southland Gallery.
hoursNote: Mon to Fri 9am to 5pm, Sat 10am to 2pm; closed Sun and public holidays; $10 adults with tasting, under 18s free

name: Eastern Southland Gallery
description:
A free art gallery in Gore's former Carnegie Library, a few steps from the visitor centre and the moonshine museum. Temporary exhibitions fill the front rooms, and behind them are one of the country's largest collections of work by Ralph Hotere, a Len Lye kinetic sculpture, and the John Money Wing, with work by Rita Angus and Theo Schoon alongside West African carvings and art from Elcho Island in Australia.

It's far better than most people expect in a small town, and easy to fit into a stop on the drive between Invercargill and Dunedin or Queenstown. It's open daily, from 1pm on Sundays and public holidays.
Local tip: Look for the giant brown trout sculpture on the way into town, since Gore calls itself the brown trout capital of the world.
hoursNote: Mon to Fri 10am to 4.30pm; Sat 10.30am to 4pm in summer, 1pm to 4pm rest of year; Sun and public holidays 1pm to 4pm; closed Good Friday, 25 and 26 December and 1 January; free entry, donations welcome

name: The Batch Cafe
description:
One of the busiest cafés in Invercargill, on Spey Street a few blocks from the centre, with several seating areas and a big cabinet of baking. It's known for good coffee and cakes, with plenty of gluten-free and dairy-free options.

Service is quick even when it's full, which it often is. It opens at 7am on weekdays and 8am at weekends, and closes at 3pm.
hoursNote: Mon to Fri 7am to 3pm; Sat and Sun 8am to 3pm; kitchen menu until 2.30pm

name: Balibu
description:
A small Indonesian food counter in the Esk Eats dining area of Invercargill Central, on Esk Street in the city centre. The fried chicken, bakso (meatball soup) and rice dishes are the favourites, and portions are big for the price.

It's open all day, every day, from 10am to 9pm, which makes it one of the more reliable cheap meals in town.
Local tip: Ask for chilli on the side, since regulars say it has a proper kick.
hoursNote: Daily 10am to 9pm; holiday hours may vary

name: TJ's Kitchen
description:
A burger and takeaway shop on St Andrew Street, known for huge burgers that can easily feed two, with generous chips. Everything is cooked to order, so there can be a short wait.

It's open from 11.30am to 8pm, Tuesday to Sunday, and 4.30pm to 8pm on Mondays, so it works for lunch or an easy dinner.
Local tip: Stick with the burgers, which get the best reviews, and share one if you're not very hungry.
hoursNote: Mon 4.30pm to 8pm; Tue to Sun 11.30am to 8pm

name: Southern Comfort Backpackers
description:
A small hostel in a well-kept colonial villa on Thomson Street, within walking distance of the city centre. It has dorms and private rooms, a cosy kitchen and lounge and a garden, and towels are included.

Reviewers praise how clean and quiet it is, and the host is full of tips, including for the ferry and hikes on Stewart Island.
Local tip: Ask about storing gear if you're heading to Stewart Island for a few days, since it's a common stop for hikers before and after the ferry.
hoursNote: Check-in from 2pm; check-out by 10am; book online

name: Invercargill Holiday Park & Motels
description:
A family-owned holiday park at 77 McIvor Road on the north side of the city, with tent and powered sites, cabins sleeping up to 6, and motel and ensuite units from about $126 a night. It's the budget option if you're not in a certified self-contained vehicle.

There's a recreation room with a kitchen, communal bathrooms, a barbecue area and a pizza oven, and reviewers rate the kitchen, bathrooms and laundry as spotless and the staff as friendly.
hoursNote: Tent, campervan, cabin and motel options

name: Colac Bay Freedom Camping
description:
A free camping area along Colac Foreshore Road at Colac Bay (Ōraka), about 45 minutes west of Invercargill, between the boat ramp and the shelter shed. You park right by the beach and fall asleep to the waves, and the bay is a popular surf spot.

Southland District Council allows certified self-contained vehicles only, with a limit of two nights in any 30 days. There's a long drop toilet, a shelter and a rubbish skip, but no drinking water. Dogs must be on a lead, fires aren't allowed, and the site is exposed to the wind, with some spots getting muddy.
Local tip: Look for a firm spot near the boat ramp after rain. The Colac Bay Bakehouse and Bar in the village does good burgers, but it's closed on Mondays and Tuesdays.
hoursNote: Certified self-contained only; max 2 nights in 30 days; long drop, shelter and skip; no water; dogs on leash; no fires

name: Stewart Island Ferry, Bluff
description:
The passenger ferry across Foveaux Strait from Bluff to Oban on Stewart Island / Rakiura, about an hour each way depending on the sea. It makes a day trip possible: over in the morning, back in the afternoon, with time for the village, its bays and the predator-free bird sanctuary on Ulva Island.

Fares are from $139, and Ulva Island trips, a village and bays tour and guided walks can be booked with the ferry. It carries no cars: there is paid parking at the Bluff terminal, and cars, vans and e-bikes to hire in Oban.
Local tip: Plan the day back from the last sailing home, and expect a lively crossing if the wind is up.
hoursNote: Stewart Island Experience terminal, 21 Foreshore Road, Bluff; about 1 hr crossing; from 1 Oct 2026 leaves Bluff 9.15am and 5.30pm and Oban 7.30am and 4pm, adding Bluff 2pm and Oban 12pm from 1 Dec; check in 30 min before; times change with the season; from $139; paid parking at the terminal
